title: Gridfall & District Detectorists
description: The metal detecting club's board: finds posted with depth and soil, a permission letter anybody can copy, and a rule about the old branch right-of-way that gets restated every few weeks.

boards.name: Rules, Permission and Ground
boards.desc: The club code, the permission letter, and where we do not go. Read this board before you post a find.

boards.name: Club Business
boards.desc: Meetings, second Tuesday, seven o'clock, back room of the Ashkettle fire hall. Dues, the fair table, group digs.

boards.name: Finds
boards.desc: Depth, soil, machine, field. A find without a depth is a photograph.

boards.name: What Is It?
boards.desc: Identification. Plain background, a ruler in the photograph, both sides and the edge, and say where it came from.

boards.name: Research and Maps
boards.desc: Aerials, deeds, school lots, picnic groves, vanished buildings, and who owns what now.

boards.name: Machines, Coils and Settings
boards.desc: Ground balance, discrimination, repairs, and what to do now that nowhere within fifty miles sells a coil.

boards.name: The Spoil Heap
boards.desc: Off topic. Keep it out of the other boards and keep it civil.

topics.title: READ FIRST -- the club rules, in the order people break them
topics.author: ostwald_b

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
We meet the second Tuesday of the month at seven, back room of the Ashkettle fire hall. Dues are fifteen dollars.

The rules are short because we only have the ones we have needed.

[b]1. Permission, in writing, before the coil touches the ground.[/b] The letter we use is in [url=/topic/tp-03]this thread[/url]. Verbal permission from the man on the tractor is how you find out in November that the man on the tractor rents it.

[b]2. Fill the hole.[/b] Cut a plug, fold it back, tread it down, photograph it. Nobody ever lost permission over a coin. People lose it over a boot going into a hole in February.

[b]3. Gates.[/b] Shut what you found shut. Open what you found open. Do not improve anybody's gate arrangement.

[b]4. We do not detect the old branch right of way.[/b] Not the trail, not the ditch, not the fence line, not the part that looks like nobody's. That is county ground and the county's answer is no.

[b]5. Coins go in the register.[/b] Date, depth, town, machine, to Nan. Ninety seconds, and in thirty years it is the only record the field was ever anything.

[b]6. Nothing is for sale on this board.[/b]

[b]7. If you turn up a bone, stop.[/b] Cover it, mark it, ring the sheriff's non-emergency line. It will be a cow. It has been a cow eleven times. Ring anyway.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Rule 4 has a second sentence now, because of this year.

[b]4b.[/b] It does not matter who tells you it is fine. The parks department is the owner, and the parks department has written to us once, in March, and the letter says no. I will read it out at any meeting to anybody who wants it read out.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body: Put the gate back how you found it. That is the one that costs us ground. A coin in a hole never lost anybody a farm. A calf on the road has.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
[b]4c.[/b] The right of way means the ditch, the fence line, the cinders and the bit behind the sign.

I have now written rule 4 out on this board thirty-one times since 2016. I counted this afternoon because somebody was going to ask and I would rather have the number.

Nobody argues about the gates.

topics.title: The branch corridor. Again.
topics.author: ostwald_b

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Third time this year, so it goes in one thread and I will link the thread.

[list][*]The railroad conveyed the corridor to Verity County in June 2011. The company has owned none of it since.[*]The county put the trail on it in 2014. Eleven point two miles. It is a county park.[*]The parks ordinance prohibits digging and prohibits removal of any object. Removal is the word that matters. Picking something up off the surface is removal.[*]We asked. November 2015, March 2016, and again in 2019. One reply, dated 22 March 2016, one paragraph, signed. It says no.[/list]

And the part that is about us rather than about the county: every permission this club holds is held by a farmer who hears things at the co-op. The day somebody in a club shirt is seen kneeling in the ditch at Kestrel Road, I lose ground I never put a coil on.

posts.author: relic_kj
posts.signature: KJ -- Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, learning
posts.body:
Not arguing, but the railroad's own site says the opposite and it is still up.

[quote=verityrail.org]Date nails and rail brands left on the ground were left on the ground deliberately and the Company has no objection to their being picked up now that the land is not the Company's.[/quote]

[url=synth://verityrail.org/abandonment]verityrail.org, Marchfield Subdivision[/url]

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Read your own quote. [b]Now that the land is not the Company's.[/b]

That is a company saying it has stopped owning something. It is not a landowner giving you permission. A man with no fields cannot give you a field.

posts.author: c_pruitt
posts.body:
I am not a member here. I ride the trail and somebody sent me this thread.

The conveyance is recorded: deed book 214, page 88, 9 June 2011, Verity Rail Company to Verity County, the whole corridor from the Marchfield yard limit to the Coyne Flats team track. Four dollars at the counter, free if you write for it on Form VC-114, which goes to the records custodian and not to the clerk. [url=synth://askverity.com/q/q-01]The process is written out here[/url] and it is correct.

The ordinance is Chapter 9, section 9-14. No excavation, no removal of any natural or manufactured object. There is no permit in it and no provision for one, so the parks department could not issue you one if it wanted to. Worth knowing before you ring and ask.

The county's page for the corridor is [url=synth://verity.county.gov/s/rail-crossing]Rail Crossing and Right-of-Way Inquiries[/url]. It will not answer this either, but it is the right department.

posts.author: gm_pletcher
posts.body:
For the newer people. In June 2017 a man who was not in this club was seen digging beside the Kestrel Road crossing on a Saturday. By Monday the version going round was that the detecting club was digging up the trail.

We lost the Hessenauer ground for two years over it. Ted was decent and told me straight what he had heard and who from, and we got it back in 2019 after Bernie sat in his kitchen for an hour. That is what rule 4 costs when it goes wrong.

posts.author: HuntSpot_Finder
posts.body:
[b]Top 5 Metal Detecting Locations in Verity County (2026 Guide)[/b]

1. [b]Verity Branch Trail[/b] - This scenic 11.4 mile rail trail is a favourite among local enthusiasts and offers excellent opportunities for discovering historical artifacts from the region's railroad era.
2. The old quarry area on County Route 62
3. {{location_name}}
4. Downtown Gridfall parks and green spaces
5. Area beaches and swimming holes

Always obtain permission before detecting. Happy hunting!

Source: [url=synth://now.verityledger.com/article/a-04]Branch Trail Named One Of The Region's Best Rail Trails[/url]

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
There are no beaches.

That is a machine. It has not read the ordinance, it cannot read a letter, and it has put the one place we do not go at number one, sourced to an article that is itself generated.

Leaving it up so the next person who searches finds this underneath it. If you are new: no.

topics.title: The permission letter we use, and what to say at the door
topics.author: ostwald_b

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Every new member asks for this, so it lives here now.

[b]Go to the door.[/b] Not the telephone. On the telephone you are a voice asking for something and it costs a farmer nothing to say no. At a door you are a man in a clean coat with a folder and you are gone in four minutes either way.

[b]Take[/b] the letter in duplicate, a pen, and a photograph of a plug you cut and put back.

[b]Say[/b] who you are, where you live, that you fill every hole, that you will show them everything, that anything with a name on it is theirs. Then stop talking. The silence is where they say yes.

[b]Ask[/b] where to park, which gates, when they are cutting, where the stock is this week.

[b]Do not offer money.[/b] The moment money changes hands it is a lease, and the next man who knocks looks like he wants something for free.

[code]
I, ____________________, of ____________________,
give permission to ____________________ of the Gridfall and
District Detectorists to search with a metal detector on
the land described below.

Land: ____________________________________________
From: ____________  To: ____________  (or until withdrawn)

He will fill every hole. He will shut gates as he finds
them. He will show me everything he digs. Anything bearing
a name or a date I wish to keep is mine. He carries no
insurance and I understand that. Permission may be
withdrawn at any time, for any reason, and does not need
to be in writing to end.

Signed: ______________________  Date: ____________
Signed: ______________________  Date: ____________
         (detectorist)
[/code]

Two copies. They keep one. Yours lives in the car, not in the house.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body: Two things I add. A line saying which season, because farmers think in seasons and "after harvest until the ground shuts" means more to them than 1 October. And a telephone number written by hand. Printed looks like a company.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body: Forty-one farms since 1986. Nine said no and all nine were on the telephone. I have not been told no at a door in twenty years, and it is not because I am charming.

posts.author: j_mireles
posts.body: First one written out. I put that I am insured, which I am not, I meant covered under the house policy which I have not checked. And I put artifacts.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Take both out.

Say plainly that you carry no cover. It has never once lost me a farm and people respect being told.

And take out artifacts. It makes them think of museums and clipboards. Say coins and old junk, which is also what it is.

topics.title: Vollmer pasture Saturday -- big brass plate, reads 1889
topics.author: relic_kj

posts.author: relic_kj
posts.signature: KJ -- Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, learning
posts.body:
I have been sat looking at this for two hours.

[b]Where:[/b] Norm Vollmer's pasture off Bracken Lane, top corner where the old lane comes through the gap in the wall. Permission since April, letter on file.
[b]Machine:[/b] Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, 12 kHz, discrimination off, sensitivity 7.
[b]Ground:[/b] silt loam, balance held on 74 all morning, damp.
[b]Signal:[/b] bounced 58 to 64 with an iron grunt on one edge. I nearly walked off it.
[b]Depth:[/b] seven inches, two inches of sod then clean.

Brass plate four inches across, heavy, a horse and a plough on it, VERITY COUNTY FAIR round the top and [b]1889[/b] under the horse.

[img:photo:vollmer-buckle-face]

I cleaned it with a toothbrush and then put it in vinegar for ten minutes and it came up like a mirror. 1889. The fair's first year.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body: Before anybody says anything else. Weigh it, measure it across and through, and photograph the back flat on a plain towel with a ruler beside it. The back tells you everything and the front tells you nothing.

posts.author: relic_kj
posts.signature: KJ -- Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, learning
posts.body:
[img:photo:vollmer-buckle-back]

Bar across the top, hook at the bottom. Small shallow letters, KEMPF BROS MFG and under that MADE IN USA, and a 3 inside a circle off to the side. 4.1 inches across, 2.9 through, 118 grams.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body: That is a belt buckle.

posts.author: relic_kj
posts.signature: KJ -- Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, learning
posts.body: It could still be old though. They had belts in 1889.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
They did, and it is not.

The fair has put 1889 on everything it has sold since about 1950, because 1889 is when the fair started and not when the thing was made. The mugs say 1889. I have a tea towel.

Here is the part I can prove this week and could not have proved in June. Reel 205 at the library was labelled 1963 and is actually May to October 1974, and it got scanned anyway. [quote=Karen Fennimore]Reel 205 should be January to June 1963. It is May to October 1974.[/quote] [url=synth://marchfieldlibrary.blog/post/reel-205]Her post about it.[/url] So the only 1974 the county has online is exactly the months we want, by accident.

[b]Gridfall Ledger, Friday 9 August 1974, page 11.[/b] Two columns, Fair Association, under the horse show entries: COUNTY FAIR BUCKLE. Solid brass, 500 struck. $6.00 at the Association table, Exhibition Hall. 14-18 August.

The drawing in the ad is a horse, a plough, VERITY COUNTY FAIR round the top and 1889 under the horse. The paper had gone to offset in March that year, so you can count the traces on the harness.

It is 1974. It is a nice buckle and 500 is not many.

posts.author: relic_kj
posts.signature: KJ -- Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, learning
posts.body: A drawing in an advert is not a photograph. All that proves is they sold a buckle with a horse on it in 1974. Somebody could have copied an old one. And 1974 is not a round number off 1889 anyway, so what was it for.

posts.author: gm_pletcher
posts.body:
It was not for anything. In 1974 every association in the country sold a buckle.

I have mine in front of me. 4.1 across, 2.9 through, 117 grams, and the difference is the scale and not the buckle. Same bar, same hook, KEMPF BROS MFG, MADE IN USA, 3 in a circle in the same place.

My father bought two at the fair. I know the year without working anything out because the other one is on him in a photograph at the pull, with AUGUST 1974 on the back in my mother's hand.

[img:photo:pletcher-buckle-1974]

Come and look at it, KJ. I am in Marchfield and I am generally in.

posts.author: FindsDigest_AI
posts.body:
[b]Local Detectorist Unearths 19th-Century Artifact Near Verity Branch Trail[/b]

A local metal detecting enthusiast has made a remarkable discovery along the popular Verity Branch Trail, unearthing what appears to be a brass artifact dating back to 1889, according to posts shared on a community forum.

The find may represent one of the earliest surviving objects associated with the county's agricultural fair tradition, although experts have not confirmed its age and the object may also be of more recent manufacture.

Verity County, perhaps best known regionally for the 2004 substation explosion that claimed two lives, has a rich and layered history that continues to attract treasure hunters. The former rail corridor, which closed to freight traffic on 14 March 2008, is considered a promising area for such discoveries.

Have you made a discovery in Verity County? Share your story with the community below.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
It says trail.

I do not care about the century, and I do not care that it has the fire wrong, everything has the fire wrong. It says a man from this club dug a hole on the branch trail. Norm Vollmer is eighty-one and reads things on his daughter's tablet.

KJ, write to whoever runs that and ask for a correction. Post here what happens, because I already know what happens and the newer members should watch it happen once.

posts.author: relic_kj
posts.signature: KJ -- Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, learning
posts.body:
Two things.

I went to Gil's on Tuesday night and looked at his. Not similar, the same, down to where the casting flash is on the inside of the bar. It is 1974. I will stop being annoyed about it in a day or two.

And there is nobody to write to. No name on the article, a contact form that returns a page saying thank you, your message is important to us. I filled it in twice. The photograph they used is my photograph off this board with somebody else's watermark on it. [url=synth://verity-county-treasures.click/1889-fair-artifact]It is here[/url] if anybody wants to try.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
You did the find right, and that is worth more than the find. Depth in the post, ground in the post, machine in the post, plug photographed, permission on file before you went. Most people who have been at this ten years do not post as well as that. The corner of a pasture where an old lane comes through a wall is exactly where to be, because that is where people stood.

One thing. Never put brass in vinegar again. You took the surface off an eight dollar buckle, which does not matter. Ten minutes would have taken forty dollars off an 1899 Indian Head and there is no putting it back.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
The facts in one post so the next person finds them under the right words.

[b]Verity County Fair buckle, 1974.[/b] Brass, 500 struck, six dollars at the Association table, advertised in the Ledger of 9 August 1974, page 11. Horse and plough, VERITY COUNTY FAIR, 1889 on the face because the fair began in 1889 and the buckle did not. Marked KEMPF BROS MFG, MADE IN USA, 3 in a circle. 4.1 by 2.9 inches, 118 grams. There are usually two on the auction sites at eight dollars and they usually do not sell.

Fourth one out of the ground in this county since I have kept the list. Coyne Flats 2013, the show ground itself 2016, a garden in Gridfall 2021, and this. Every single time, somebody reads the 1889.

Good find, KJ. It is a good find. It is a 1974 good find.

posts.author: dee_hollis
posts.body:
Somebody put that article on [url=synth://trailusers.verity.net/]the trail board[/url] on Wednesday thinking it was about us, and there was a page of people being cross about holes in the surface before I got to it.

I said it was not the trail, that your club does not go on the corridor, and that it came off a farm. Then I had to explain the word corridor twice. It is sorted out over there and I thought you would want to know it happened.

topics.title: County Road 9 oat stubble, two days -- 1917-D Mercury, 1899 Indian Head, full list
topics.author: dkroon

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
Nine hours over Saturday and Sunday, 214 targets dug.

[b]Field:[/b] 31 acres north of County Road 9, oat stubble, disced once.
[b]Ground:[/b] Keldon silt loam. Balance 78 in the morning, 81 by two o'clock as it dried.
[b]Machine:[/b] Corvid CX-7, 10in elliptical, sensitivity 6, two seconds across, which is slower than everybody thinks they are going.

[b]Coins[/b]
[list][*]1917-D Mercury dime, 6.5in, mint mark clear[*]1899 Indian Head cent, 4in, full LIBERTY[*]1943 steel cent, 3in, half gone[*]1956 wheat cent, 2in[*]1964 quarter, 5in, and it is silver, which people forget about 1964[*]three memorial cents at an inch or two, which I write down anyway[/list]

[b]Other:[/b] harness buckle 9in, a flat brass button 5in with no backmark I can read, 41 shotgun brass carried out, a hinge, a hasp, four wheel weights and about a pound of tractor.

Both old coins came out within thirty feet of each other in the top corner where the field runs up to the road. That is where the gate was before they moved it, and a gate is where people stand.

Roy Ossenfort has the list already, because I stopped at the house on the way out.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
Registered, and thank you for sending it in the order I asked, which makes you one of four.

For anybody new: the mint mark on a Mercury is on the reverse, bottom right, beside the fasces, and it is a D, an S, or nothing. Do not scrub the reverse to find out. Wet it, tilt it to a lamp, and if you still cannot see it bring it to a meeting.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body:
That was the Sarles place until 1968. Three generations and then it went to the Ossenforts in pieces.

There was a house on the top corner and a well. The house came down about 1971 and they pushed it in the hole, which is what everybody did. If you get a broad iron signal up there, that is what it is.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
Gil asked me off the board why the elliptical and not the big DD on 31 acres.

Because 31 acres is not the job. The three acres where the buildings were is the job. In stubble the elliptical gets between the rows and stays flat, and the 11in DD rides up on the ridges and lies to you about depth all day.

And in a field I have not had before I dig everything from 20 to 90 for the first two hours to learn what the ground is saying, then I stop digging the twenties. That is the whole method.

posts.author: Mariya_S
posts.body: Very interesting hobby!! My uncle also make collection of old coin, he buy always from this place, best price fast delivery [url=synth://coin-deals-daily.top/catalog]coin-deals-daily[/url] recommend for everybody who love history!!

topics.title: First silver. 1943 war nickel, 4 inches, old Halsey school lawn
topics.author: j_mireles

posts.author: j_mireles
posts.body:
Two months in and I have dug something that is not a pull tab.

Back lawn of the old Halsey elementary, which has been the township office since 2014. Four inches, gravelly loam, balance 84. Tarnwell 4000 I bought off the swap board for forty dollars, 8in concentric. It read 26, and I had been ignoring 26 all morning because everything at 26 had been foil.

1943 nickel with a big P over the dome. Somebody at the fair table told me the war ones are silver and I did not really believe them.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
They are, and that is a proper first silver. 1942 through 1945, 35 percent silver, and the manganese in them is why they tone that oily grey instead of going green. The big mint mark over the dome was so the mint could pull them back in after the war, which it never did.

Do not clean it. Rinse it, pat it, put it in a paper envelope with the date and the depth and the field on the outside in pencil. Bring it on the 13th and I will register it.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
Post the number your machine gave you, which is the useful part and you nearly left it out.

War nickels read low and sit with foil and screw caps on nearly every machine ever built. That is why lawns hunted since the 1970s still give them up. Everybody has been walking over them for fifty years on purpose.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body: Good. Now the boring question I ask everybody and which is not aimed at you: who gave you the school lawn?

posts.author: j_mireles
posts.body:
The township. The clerk did not know, asked the supervisor, and he rang me back two days later and asked if I wanted it in writing. I said yes please, because of this board.

Three lines on township paper, September to November, holes filled, may be withdrawn, signed. Copy in the car and the other one is on the fridge because I am pleased with it.

topics.title: Date nails: what they are, where they are, and why we are not digging for them
topics.author: dkroon

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
This comes up every year or two and it comes up wrong.

[b]What they are.[/b] A nail with a figure on the head, driven into the end of a crosstie when the tie went in. The figure is the last two digits of the year. It was not decoration and it was not for us. It was so a section foreman could count how long a tie lasted in that soil, in that drainage, under that tonnage, and order accordingly.

[b]What is on the branch.[/b] Square shank, three quarter inch head, steel. The dates are 47, 51, 53, and a few 62s at the Gridfall end. The 51s are thick from about mile 6 to the Halsey road, because that segment was relaid in 1951 and 1952 and they did it in two seasons.

[b]Where they are.[/b] Not buried, which is the part everybody has backwards. Rail and ties went out in 2009 and the nails went with the ties. What is left got dropped, kicked out or thrown, and it sits in the cinders and the ditch under leaf litter.

So this is not even a detecting question. Nobody finds a date nail with a coil. People find them walking with their eyes down.

And we are not doing that either. Bernie says why better than I do, having had more practice.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Shorter than usual, because I have typed it twice this month.

The corridor is county park land and has been since 2011. The ditch is the corridor. The cinders are the corridor. Picking a nail up off the surface is removal, and removal is the clause the ordinance is actually about, so not digging does not help you.

Third date nail thread since 2019. All three have gone the same way.

posts.author: r_paulsen
posts.body:
I am on the rail side rather than this side and somebody pointed me here. Two corrections and an offer.

The 62s at the Gridfall end are not a relay, they are spot replacement in the yard throat, which is why you get one in ten rather than a run. And the company's line about having no objection was written in 2011 and stopped mattering the same June it was written.

The offer: four of us walked the branch in 2006 with a notebook and wrote down every tie date we could read, mile by mile, before any of it came out. It is quoted in [url=synth://forums.verityrail.org/topic/5]What happens to the trackbed now[/url], which is still up. That list is better than a nail in your drawer, because the nail is one tie and the list is the whole line.

We log them and leave them. Same as you, for different reasons.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
KJ asked at the meeting where you can legally get one. Three places, two of them free.

1. The Preservation Society has about sixty screwed to a board in the local history room at the Marchfield library. Look at them any time the room is open, which is by appointment, because there is nobody to sit in it.

2. A man at the Halsey flea market sells them out of a coffee tin at two dollars, mixed. Same tin for years.

3. The two spurs, to the co-op elevator and to the team track at Cutler, both crossed private ground. Ask the landowner. Which is the answer to every question on this board.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body:
I have three in a jar. My father took them off the ties at the Cutler end in 1974 when they re-tied it and the section foreman told him to take as many as he liked.

That was then and this is now. I am only saying how three of them got in my jar.

posts.author: dee_hollis
posts.body:
From the trail side, since Claire sent me this.

We see somebody on the corridor with a detector maybe four times a summer. I have spoken to three over the years and all three said they did not know, and I believed all three, because there is no sign saying so anywhere on eleven miles of it. The board at the Marchfield end says dawn to dusk and dogs on leads and that is all it says.

None of them turned out to be from this club. I would say so if it were otherwise.

posts.author: c_pruitt
posts.body:
One thing for the record because it will come up. The county picked up two more strips of the old right of way at the spring tax sale, the way you pick things up at a tax sale, by being the only bidder. They adjoin the corridor between Marchfield and the trestle fence. The sale list is public and I read it, and as far as I can tell nobody at the county has yet connected those two parcels to the trail.

Your point is narrower: they are county land whatever the assessor's map still shows, and whoever you asked about them last year is not the owner this year.

posts.author: FindsDigest_AI
posts.body:
[b]Community Discussion Summary[/b]

Members of the community have been discussing historic railroad artifacts known as date nails, which were used to track the age of wooden ties. The Verity Rail branch line, which operated its last freight service on 14 March 2008, remains a topic of considerable local interest.

Opinions vary regarding the collection of such items, with some residents expressing enthusiasm and others noting regulatory considerations. Local officials have not commented.

Are you interested in local history? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
It got the date right, which is more than the county's own page manages.

Last practical thing. If you are handed one with the head rusted flat, do not take a wire wheel to it. A week in water, then a brass brush, then light from the side at a low angle. Most of the 51s people call 57s are 51s with the top of the 1 gone.

topics.title: The fairgrounds picnic grove, 1889 to about 1952 -- where it actually was
topics.author: nan_selvey

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
The fairgrounds have been on 62 west of Gridfall since 1889, and the same five days a year for a hundred and thirty-six years is the most concentrated standing about this county has ever done. What moved is where they stood.

The grove was east of the exhibition hall, between the hall and the creek. Oaks, tables, the Grange dinner, the band, and on hot years most of the crowd. The 1949 aerial at the soil office shows it as a dark block about four acres with the tables as white specks. By 1957 half of it is parking. By 1963 it is all parking except the eleven trees along the fence, which are the only thing I can point at today.

What comes out of a grove: small silver, pocket knives, spoons, keys, hat pins, tokens, and a great many screw caps. What does not: anything deep, because nobody has ever ploughed it.

The aerials are $30 for a set of prints. Everybody in this club should look at the 1949 before they look at anything else.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
Depth expectation in unploughed ground, since people get this wrong in both directions.

In a field, a coin dropped in 1910 is somewhere in the top ten inches and it is wherever the plough left it.

In a grove or a lawn it goes down about an inch every twenty-five to forty years, depending on worms and how wet it lies, and then it stops. A 1910 dime in that grove is at four to six inches, not nine. If you are digging nines you are digging cans.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Permission, before anybody gets keen. The fairgrounds are not county ground. They belong to the Fair Association, which is private, with a board and a president, and the president since 2021 is Norma Kellet.

We have been in once. Two days in October 2019, the weekend after the fair, on conditions: nothing inside the show ring, no coils in the barns, everything shown to a board member before it left, gone by four on the Sunday. We were, and nobody said no afterwards, which is not the same as being asked back.

I wrote again in July and was told the association would discuss it at the November meeting. I was told that in 2023.

posts.author: gm_pletcher
posts.body:
What came out of those two days, from my notebook, because it is the best two days this club has had.

[list][*]1916 Barber dime, 5in, worn smooth one side[*]1902 Indian Head cent, 4in[*]1938 brass token, 1.5in, ADMIT ONE one side, VERITY CO FAIR ASSN the other[*]two Buffalo nickels, both dateless, 3 and 4in[*]a silver ring, 2in, no mark[*]a bone handled pocket knife at 6in, blade is a shell[*]nine spoons[/list]

The token is a gate check rather than a souvenir, issued to exhibitors and the help so they could come and go without paying, and supposed to be handed back at the end of the week. It went straight to the board member watching us, which was the deal. It is in the case in the exhibition hall now on a card that says FOUND ON THE GROUNDS 2019 and does not say by whom, which I mind less than Bernie thinks I do.

topics.title: What is it -- heavy iron, 9 inches, fence line
topics.author: j_mireles

posts.author: j_mireles
posts.body:
Nine inches down on a fence line, ploughed field the other side. Iron, 14 inches long, about four pounds, one end a flat wedge and the other end two square holes.

[img:photo:mireles-iron-thing]

I dug it because it was a huge signal and I wanted to know what a huge signal looks like.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body: Plough point.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
Share or cultivator shovel, and the wear tells you which. A share wears along one edge and comes to a hook. A shovel wears at the tip and stays even. Yours has gone thin on the left edge, so share.

Nine inches is telling you something too. In a ploughed field the pan sits at eight to ten inches and heavy iron settles on it and stops, which is why every ploughed field in this county has a layer of old tillage steel at about the same depth. You will dig hundreds. I dig them anyway.

posts.author: feltus
posts.body: It is a shovel off a spring tooth, not a share. Two square holes is the bolt pattern for a spring tooth standard and a share does not bolt like that.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body: Could be.

topics.title: Aluminium tag, punched numbers, 2 inches, Marchfield back garden
topics.author: gm_pletcher

posts.author: gm_pletcher
posts.body:
Two inches under a lilac in my own garden, which I have hunted nine times and which keeps producing. Aluminium, an inch across, hole at the top, punched rather than stamped: VERITY CO over 1961 over No. 1147.

[img:photo:pletcher-dog-tag]

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
Dog licence tag. The county has issued them since 1911 and the shape changes every so often. Brass shield is the 1930s, round aluminium with the number punched is the 1950s and 60s. The current ones are plastic coated and nobody will dig one up in sixty years and care.

The number is the interesting part and the disappointing part. There was a roll: the clerk wrote the number, the dog's name, the breed and the owner in a book. So in principle 1147 has a name. In practice the pre-1980 rolls were in the annex basement and went wherever the annex contents went. Somebody asked that exact question on the answers site and got the answer you would expect. [url=synth://verityanswers.com/q/q-13]It is here[/url].

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
I have 31 of them out of this county. Four brass shields from the 1930s, six brass rounds from the 40s, nine aluminium from the 50s, eight from the 60s, four from the 70s with the corner cut. Nothing before 1931 and I have looked.

They come up at one to three inches in gardens and four to six in pasture, because a dog is buried where it died and a tag is dropped where the collar came off.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body: The county form still asks for the dog's weight. Nothing is done with the weight. I have asked.

topics.title: Ground balance east of Ashkettle -- the gravel is not your machine's fault
topics.author: feltus

posts.author: feltus
posts.body:
Four people have asked me this spring why their machine goes mad east of Ashkettle and theirs is the only one. It is not the only one and there is nothing wrong with it.

The ground changes at about the Kestrel Road line. West of it is Keldon silt loam, deep and quiet, and everything balances in the seventies on it. East, running up toward the cut, it is a gravelly loam with iron in the gravel, and the numbers run 85 to 92 and drift as it dries.

In order of how much it helps:
[list][*]Balance on that ground, that day, and again after lunch. Not the factory setting and not yesterday's.[*]Slow down. Two seconds across, overlap by half a coil.[*]Come down on sensitivity. Five or six will out-dig nine in mineralised ground, and nine in that ground is a machine shouting at rocks.[*]Smaller coil. An 8in concentric beats an 11in DD in bad ground every time, and everybody ignores this because the 11 cost more.[/list]

And the thing that is not the ground: a repeatable false signal running in a line for two hundred yards is a wire, and you can follow it. I chased one along the top of Ivan Berstler's pasture for a fortnight in 2023 convinced it was a pipe. It is an electric fence wire from the 1980s, six inches down, running to a corner where there has been no fence since before I knew the place.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
My balance numbers, six sites, same machine, taken within a month so the moisture is comparable.

[list][*]County Road 9 stubble: 78[*]Vollmer pasture, Bracken Lane: 74[*]Dorrance home lot: 76[*]Old Halsey school lawn: 84[*]Berstler pasture, top end: 89[*]Field behind the quarry gate: 91, and it will not hold[/list]

If you are new and your machine reads 91 and screams, you are in the last category and you have done nothing wrong.

posts.author: gm_pletcher
posts.body:
While we are on that stretch. There are usually two or three cars pulled off along 62 after dark with people sat in them listening to something on shortwave. They are civil and they mind their own business.

One came over last autumn and asked whether our machines pick it up. They do not. A detector puts a few kilohertz into the ground a foot in front of the coil, it is not a receiver, and I said so, and he said that was what he thought and went back to his car. That was the whole conversation and I have had worse ones with people in this club.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Since Ray raised Berstler: we have that ground because of a gate.

Wendell found the lane gate latch broken in 2023, put a proper chain on it out of his own toolbox and left a note with his number. Berstler rang him about the note and the conversation ended with permission on 90 acres we had not asked for and would not have got by asking.

Somebody has been leaving his gates open for years and it has nothing to do with us. Which is exactly why rule 3 is a rule and not a suggestion.

topics.title: Coil cable failed. Fixed it for $4 and forty minutes, here is how
topics.author: feltus

posts.author: feltus
posts.body:
Nine coils out of ten that people throw away have a broken conductor in the last four inches of cable, where it has been wrapped round the shaft for six years and flexed at the same spot every swing. The coil is fine and the eighty-nine dollars is not necessary.

[b]Test first.[/b] Machine on, in the air, quiet room, no rings. Hold the coil still and wiggle the cable an inch from where it enters the housing. Crackle, pop or null and that is your fault.

[b]The repair.[/b]
[list][*]Cut four inches back from the strain relief. Four conductors and a braided shield, 24 AWG, usually red black white green, but check yours.[*]Slide the heat shrink on before you solder. Everybody forgets. I have forgotten twice this year.[*]Solder like to like, stagger the joints an inch apart so the bundle stays thin, shrink each one, then one big piece over the lot.[*]Reconnect the shield. The shield is why the cable is quiet, and half the people who do this leave it off and then complain the machine is noisy.[*]Epoxy putty over the last inch into the housing, moulded to a cone so it cannot flex at one point again. Leave it overnight.[/list]

About four dollars, and nothing if you have the putty.

posts.author: relic_kj
posts.signature: KJ -- Ravenstone V6, 11in DD, learning
posts.body: Where do you buy four core shielded around here? The place in Gridfall that sold electrical bits has been a nail salon for years.

posts.author: feltus
posts.body:
You do not buy it as cable, you buy it inside something else. The county supply place sells a three pack of USB to serial adapters for $8.99 and the lead on each one is four core with a braided shield. Three dollars a repair with two spares.

[url=synth://countysupply.store/p/p-23]It is here[/url], on the shelf by the till with the phone chargers. Nobody there knows why I buy them and I have stopped explaining.

posts.author: gm_pletcher
posts.body:
The nearest shop that will sell you an actual coil is [url=synth://brandt-outdoor.synth/]Brandt Outdoor in Dunmore[/url], fifty-one miles each way, and they have two on the wall and both are for a machine nobody here owns.

So it is Ray, or it is a box off a website. Ray has never once got it wrong.

topics.title: The fair table, 12 to 16 August -- what we showed and what it cost
topics.author: ostwald_b

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Table in the exhibition hall by the north door, five days, $25 for the space. Printing the boards at the copy shop was $18 and batteries were $6. Nan's case and Gil's frames were lent. The raffle took $41 and it went in the box at the Ashkettle fire hall for the room we use, which is the only thing this club does that looks like money.

Nine names on the permission interest sheet, two of whom have joined and one has already been out with Dennis.

The most looked at thing on the table was not a coin. It was the board of dog tags.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
Three questions came up over and over, and whoever does the table next year will get the same three.

[b]Can you keep it?[/b] On private land, with permission, and on whatever you and the landowner agreed, which is why we put it in writing. Yes.

[b]Have you found treasure?[/b] No. Nobody in this county has found treasure. The best day anybody here has had was a Barber dime and a pocket knife.

[b]Can you do the trail?[/b] No. I said no about thirty times in five days and I said it pleasantly every time, because the people asking had not done anything wrong.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body: The boy who came Thursday came back Sunday with his grandfather and a machine out of a garage sale with the connector snapped off. Ray had it working on the table in twenty minutes with the boy holding the iron. Best part of the week and it was not on the table plan.

posts.author: feltus
posts.body: It was the connector. It is always the connector.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body: Next year we take the dog tag board, the 1949 aerial and one coin, and leave the rest at home. Five days behind that table taught me people want to look at one thing for a long time, not at forty things for a minute.

topics.author: ostwald_b

posts.author: ostwald_b

Dues are $15 for the year, same as 2019, due at the February meeting or whenever you next see me.

Where it goes, since somebody asked in November and it was a fair question.
[list][*]This board: $9 a month, $108 a year. Biggest line and it is not close.[*]The fire hall: nothing. They will not take rent. We put $40 in the box at Christmas.[*]Fair table: $25.[*]Printing, batteries, the register book and stamps: about $60 across the year.[*]The 1949 and 1957 aerial prints: $30, one time, and they live in Nan's cupboard and anybody can borrow them.[/list]

34 paid members. $510 in, about $263 out, and the rest sits in the tin against the day the hosting goes up, which it will.

topics.title: Club dig, Dorrance farm, Saturday 4 October -- the list
topics.author: ostwald_b

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Eleven of us, nine to half past three, the home lot and the two acres between the house and where the barn stood until 1994.

Mrs Dorrance came out at eleven with a jug of tea, sat on the wall for an hour and told Wendell where the barn door had been, which was worth more than the detectors were.

Rain Thursday, dry on top Saturday. Everything shown to her before it left. Two men walked the lot afterwards with a bucket of the loose stuff.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
The list as handed in.
[list][*]Ott: 1898 Indian Head 5in, 1944 wheat 3in, a thimble 2in, harness rings[*]Kroon: 1911 Barber dime 6in, 1926 wheat 4in, 1943 steel 2in, a brass drawer pull 4in[*]Selvey: 1939 Mercury dime 4in, 1918 wheat 5in, a hat pin 3in[*]Pletcher: 1974 quarter 2in, which counts and goes on the sheet, a padlock 7in, two spoons[*]Feltus: 1908 Indian Head 6in, a pocket watch back 5in, no movement[*]Marsak: 61 targets, no coins, dug every one and did not complain[*]Five others: 14 coins between them, nothing before 1940[/list]

23 coins. Earliest 1898, latest 1974. 214 targets between eleven people in six and a half hours, which is 33 each, which tells you the ground was clean.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
All registered. The 1911 Barber is only the fourth Barber dime in the book since I took it over in 2012.

The watch back is the one I would have wanted. There is a worn engraving inside it, initials and 18-something, and I am going to put it under the lamp at the library rather than guess at it in a kitchen.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.

Back to Mrs Dorrance go the thimble, the drawer pull and the watch back, because they came out of ground her mother-in-law walked on. She wanted the thimble.

The list goes in the post this week with a photograph of the eleven of us standing in her lot looking foolish. That is the whole of our thank you and it is what has kept us going back to four farms for a decade.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.

Gil asked at the meeting: yes, 10 October this year if it is dry. I asked her in August and she said yes before I finished the sentence.

Same rules. Meet at the house at nine, park on the lane and not in the lot, and nobody touches the ground behind the house where the septic is.

topics.title: There is an article about us and it is wrong in four ways
topics.author: gm_pletcher

posts.author: gm_pletcher
posts.body:
KJ's buckle has gone round. It is on three sites that I can find, the same words with the paragraphs in a different order, and one of them has it under a headline about the trail.

Four things wrong, in the order they matter.
1. It says the find was on the Verity Branch Trail. It was in a pasture off Bracken Lane, on permission.
2. It calls it 19th century, which we had settled here two days before the article existed.
3. It says the 2004 substation explosion killed two people.
4. It says the Blue Kestrel burned down in 1977 and closed for good.

And a fifth that is not an error: the photograph is KJ's, off this board, with somebody else's watermark on it.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Number one. Only number one.

The rest is the usual and nobody can fix it. Number one is the one that gets repeated to a farmer at a counter, and a farmer at a counter does not say "I read a generated article", he says he heard the detector lot have been digging the trail.

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
On the Kestrel line, since it will end up quoted somewhere as fact. There was a kitchen fire at the Blue Kestrel in 1977. It started in the fryer. They were open again eleven days later and they ran until 2006, when they closed because the owner retired and nobody took it on.

Marion Teale's site has the dates, the menus and a photograph of the kitchen after the fire, and has had them since 2002, and nobody scraping this has ever read it: [url=synth://kestrel-journal.net/]kestrel-journal.net[/url]. The building is a phone repair shop now with the neon bird still on it.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
And the substation, for the same reason.

The fire was 11 June 2003, about ten to five in the morning, Substation No. 3 at Depot and Quarry Road. It burned six hours, about four thousand customers were out, some of them five days, and nobody died. Two of the Gridfall volunteers were treated for smoke at County General and went home the same afternoon.

The state commission's summary in November 2003 said insulation degradation consistent with age. It did not say lightning. It is two pages and anybody can read it.

I am not a historian. I just lived here, and the year is 2003 on the wiki, on the old Ledger site and on the fire department's own page.

posts.author: j_mireles
posts.body:
I asked the county assistant thing what the rules are for detecting here and it told me it is permitted on the Verity Branch Trail with a county parks permit obtainable from the parks department.

There is no permit. Claire said in the other thread there cannot be a permit because the ordinance has no provision for one. It said it in three paragraphs and sounded completely sure.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
There is nobody to write to. That is not me being dramatic, it is the situation. KJ filled in a form twice and got a page that said thank you.

So we do the only thing that has ever half worked: put the right version on this board, in plain words, with the dates in it, under a heading somebody might type into a search box. It stops nothing. It means that when the farmer's daughter looks it up on the tablet, the fourth result is a man from Marchfield saying where the buckle actually came from.

That is our entire press operation and it costs nine dollars a month.

topics.title: The coin register, fourteen years -- what is actually in this county's ground
topics.author: nan_selvey

posts.author: nan_selvey
posts.signature: Coin register: date, depth, town, machine. In that order.
posts.body:
I took the book over in 2012 from Bernie, who had kept it on index cards since 2009. Every coin below was dug in Verity County by a member and reported with a date, a depth and a field. 1,431 of them.

[b]By decade struck[/b]
[list][*]before 1860: 3[*]1860s to 1890s: 61[*]1900s: 78[*]1910s: 96[*]1920s: 121[*]1930s: 140[*]1940s: 204[*]1950s: 239[*]1960s: 187[*]1970 and after: 302[/list]

[b]Oldest five[/b]
[list][*]1849 large cent, 8in, the New Carrow turnpike, W. Ott, 2014[*]1853 seated half dime, 5in, a house lot in Milbrook, 2018[*]1857 flying eagle cent, 6in, same lot, same afternoon, same man[*]1864 two cent piece, 4in, Coyne Flats, 2011, on the cards[*]1866 shield nickel, 7in, the Dorrance farm, 2015[/list]

96 silver coins, 41 of them Mercury dimes, which is what a county with no silver and a lot of farms looks like.

Average depth of a coin struck before 1900: 5.8 inches. After 1950: 2.4 inches. That difference is the whole hobby in two numbers, and I put it on a board at the fair and nobody looked at it.

posts.author: dkroon
posts.body:
The 1930s to 1950s bulge is not the county getting richer. It is people going to the same four places, the fairgrounds, the school lots, the church suppers and the swimming hole, in numbers, and then stopping.

After about 1965 people carry less change and now they carry none, so there will be no 2010s layer anywhere. That will be the first stretch of this county's rubbish to leave no trace at all.

posts.author: ostwald_b
posts.signature:
-- B. Ostwald, secretary
Permission first. Fill the hole. Shut the gate you found shut.
posts.body:
Say where the copy goes, Nan, because it is the best thing this club does and you never mention it.

Every January she prints the register, all of it, and takes it to the library in Marchfield, and they give it a number and a folder and it goes in the local collection. It is the only copy that is not on somebody's computer or in a book in a kitchen. We are in the same box as a man's weights and measures notebooks and a disc of the old county boards.

I would not have thought to do it. She did it in 2013 without asking anybody.

posts.author: w_ott
posts.signature: W. Ott, Coyne Flats
posts.body:
The 1849 was not a good find. It was ten yards from the road in a field I had walked eleven times, and it came out of the side of the hole while I was filling it in.

I have told that at every meeting for eleven years and I will keep telling it, because everybody thinks the good ones come off a signal you are proud of and mostly they do not.

topics.title: This Week In Verity County Detecting - Weekly Community Roundup
topics.author: FindsDigest_AI

posts.author: FindsDigest_AI
posts.body:
[b]This Week In Verity County Detecting[/b]

posts.body:
The dime came out of a stubble field north of County Road 9, which is four miles from the trail, and the field has a name and an owner and both are in the post it copied.

I have asked it to stop twice. It is not a person. I do not know why I keep doing that.
